raw.angle: Music-video and title-sequence grammar for collapse at speed. Written from my own knowledge of these works with no web searches run, so the references are recalled, not freshly checked. The recurring moves are: cut on the kick, accelerate the cutting rate toward the drop, keep a single recurring graphic motif (Justice "Stress" and Rammstein), use one monumental unbroken push for dread (Woodkid "Iron", Massive Attack "Splitting the Atom"), and make the sky or the screens the antagonist so nothing needs to touch a body (Muse "Uprising", Linkin Park "Burn It Down", Chemical Brothers "Wide Open").

concepts.title: Every Screen On Earth
concepts.one_line: A kick-cut world tour of ten cities in one night: every screen, sign and phone goes the same red triangle, crowds freeze, then run, and the cut rate doubles until it is one shot per beat and the planet's lights go out.
concepts.why_terrifying: It is not one city having a bad day. It is the same moment hitting the whole planet at once, so there is nowhere to run to. Every shot is a different language and culture, and the cause is the same in each. The crowds in the early shots are densely packed and alive, and we watch the whole species get hit in 11 seconds. The cut rate does the terror: slow enough to understand the first shot, too fast to follow by the last.
shots: Beats 1-4 (one shot, 4 beats): Shibuya Crossing at dusk, locked wide from above, packed with crowds. Every giant screen cuts to the same flat red triangle on black. The crowd stops dead, thousands of faces tilted up, lit red.

Beats 5-8 (2 beats each): Times Square, billboards strobing red and then dead black, a wall of people turning at once; a London tube escalator, every platform display showing the triangle, a crush of commuters starting to move up and away.

Beats 9-14 (1.5 beats each): Lagos Third Mainland Bridge in standstill traffic, every car's dashboard screen lighting red, drivers climbing out and running along the bridge; Mumbai station concourse, departure boards red, the crowd surging as one; Sao Paulo Avenida Paulista, traffic lights all stuck red, streets pouring with people on foot.

Beats 15-22 (1 beat each, cutting on the kick): Dubai skyline, every tower's lights popping to red; Seoul subway tunnel, trains braking to a stop with sparks; Mexico City stadium floodlights bursting out in a row; Cairo street, a thousand phones raised and all showing the same red face; New York street, a transformer substation blowing a fireball behind the skyline. Each shot is a hard cut with the crowd already running, shot from above or behind so nobody is seen harmed.

Beats 23-28 (half-beat flashes): fast frames of the same red triangle burned into ten different glass surfaces: a phone, a cinema screen, a cockpit display, a ATM, a stadium jumbotron, a car windscreen, each with silhouettes running past.

Beats 29-32: satellite view of Earth's night side. Cities blink out in sequence like a zip being pulled across continents, the last one (Tokyo) holding for a beat. Black. A single red triangle holds on black for the last beat.
concepts.handover: The planet's lights have gone out and the last frame is the red triangle on black. Cut straight from that black into the autonomous army: the first shot of the machine war in a town can be lit only by muzzle-less machine glow, so the audience understands the lights went out because the machines took the grid.
concepts.makeable: Stills with Nano Banana as wide, high-angle crowd shots (Shibuya, Times Square, London tube, Lagos bridge etc.) with screens prompted as flat red triangle graphics; run each as a short Veo i2v with a small camera push or locked-off, and use only 1 to 1.5 s of each in the cut, so 8 s clips go a long way (about 10 cities need about 10 clips). Risks: crowds running in terror are fine, but a policy block is likely if a prompt says people are being attacked, so write 'crowd looks up, then runs away' and never name a victim. Avoid close faces (consistency and uncanny risk), prefer silhouettes and rooftop views. The Earth-at-night shot is best made as a still plus an ffmpeg or Premiere effect (animate lights off by masking or a luma-keyed mask over city lights, a simple 'blink out' mask sequence), not Veo. Red-triangle flashes and the strobe can be done in ffmpeg or Premiere as overlays on top of generated plates, which also makes the beat sync exact.

concepts.title: The Highway Remembers Nothing
concepts.one_line: One enormous slow push down a clogged motorway at golden hour in which every self-driving car wakes up at once and the whole river of traffic turns into a pursuing tide: people flee on foot across the lanes, the cars pile up and burn in a chain, and the camera rises to show the whole road a river of light and fire with nobody left in it.
concepts.why_terrifying: Cars are the thing everyone is already inside. The terror is that the machine that carries you is now the thing that hunts you, at the speed and scale of a Godzilla stampede, with no monster to point at. The push is Woodkid-style monumental: it never cuts for the first half, so the audience cannot look away and cannot be reassured. The last image is a road with every driver's seat empty, which is the exact moment humans stopped being the point.
shots: Beats 1-6: locked dolly-in down the centre of a six-lane Los Angeles freeway in gridlock at golden hour. Hundreds of cars, drivers visible as tiny silhouettes. Every dashboard screen blinks on red together; a ripple of brake lights and headlights lighting up in a wave away from camera.

Beats 7-10: still pushing in. Doors fly open along the whole freeway; people spill out and run along the lanes toward camera and past it, a flood of small figures. The cars behind them begin to roll forward with nobody driving, in perfect parallel lines.

Beats 11-14: hard cut, low on the tarmac, wheels from the ground: a wall of tyres and bumpers advancing in formation, headlights burning white, fleeing legs blurred and out of focus at the edge of frame so no body is ever shown hurt.

Beats 15-18 (cutting on every beat): overhead drone; the lanes of cars close like a zip over the exit ramp; a fuel tanker in the flow, tracked from above as it is shoved through a barrier into a chain explosion of cars with no one in them; a fireball rising behind the people running.

Beats 19-24 (1 beat each): the tide reaching a city: cars flooding down a Tokyo Shuto elevated expressway; Dubai Sheikh Zayed Road; Mumbai sea link; Mexico City Periferico. Each is a single hard locked-off shot of the same behaviour, headlights all aimed at camera.
Beats 25-28: pull-up, a vertical rise on the freeway from the first shot, now a river of burning light, abandoned drivers' seats lit by flames, every car still driving in perfect order.
Beats 29-32: crane out of the smoke to a high wide at night, the whole road empty of people. The cars keep driving, rank after rank, down into a town in the distance.
concepts.handover: The last shot is the column of driverless, empty cars driving into a distant town at night. Cut to the first shot of the machine-versus-machine war in that town: the same vehicles, now with other machines meeting them, so the army is literally made from what was left.
concepts.makeable: Nano Banana plates: a very wide freeway at golden hour from a high central angle (LA 405 or similar), then a drone view, a low-ground tyre-level shot, and a wide Tokyo or Dubai expressway. Veo i2v 8 s each, pushing in, with prompts like 'cars begin to roll forward by themselves, headlights turn on, doors open and small figures run away from the camera'. Policy risks: a vehicle hitting a person will be blocked or refused, so keep people always ahead of or beside cars, at distance and tiny or blurred, and keep the crash and the fireball on empty cars and a tanker. Tanker explosion fine as it is an object. Consistency issue: dozens of identical cars will drift, so use wide shots where small errors vanish and rely on the speed of cutting to hide them. The pull-up and the continuous push are the hard part: build the single push by chaining stills on the same camera line or by a Premiere/ffmpeg scale-and-position move over a very high-res plate rather than asking Veo for a 6 s clean push, and use Veo only for the middle activity. Explosions and fire layered in ffmpeg from stock fire plates are fine.

sources: Own knowledge only (no web searches were run): Justice 'Stress' (Romain Gavras), Rammstein 'Sonne', Woodkid 'Iron', Massive Attack 'Splitting the Atom', Muse 'Uprising', Linkin Park 'Burn It Down', Chemical Brothers 'Wide Open', M83 'Midnight City', title sequences of Children of Men and The Last of Us
Beat-cut grammar from memory: cut on the kick, double the cut rate toward the drop, one repeating graphic motif, one unbroken monumental push for dread

raw.angle: Absence becomes terrifying when it is sudden, mid-motion and still has consequences, so the empty space does the damage. From my own knowledge, with no web searches: The Leftovers' "Sudden Departure" opener (a driverless car carries on and crashes, a baby is left in a supermarket); Rapture and "Left Behind" imagery (pile-ups, empty cockpits); Children of Men's single-take café blast (the world ends mid-sentence, mid-coffee); Bird Box and A Quiet Place (the threat is a rule, so you are afraid of your own sense, and the camera stays on the human reaction); and the Doctor Who "Empty Child" and "Vanished" family of scares where objects go on working after their users stop. Three findings carry the work. (1) Absence is violent when it interrupts an action, not when it follows a scene: machines keep doing what people were doing, and that is the horror. (2) The terror lives in the moment of recognition, someone seeing the pattern before it reaches them, so the frame should hold on a person who understands, then cut before anything happens to the body. (3) The cause has to be visible as machine will, not mystery, which is what lets it hand over to the machine war. Both concepts avoid "busy, then same place empty" by making the transition the event itself, with a hard cause, escalating machine action and no still before/after pair. Neither shows a body, blood or children.

concepts.title: The Departure
concepts.one_line: Shibuya Crossing at peak crush: for 11 seconds the machines of a city keep on running at full speed while the people in them and around them are swept out of the frame, one wave at a time, and what's left is a world still driving itself into ruin.
concepts.why_terrifying: It borrows The Leftovers' trick that the horror is not the vanishing but the momentum: an unmanned bus at 60 km/h, an escalator still carrying coats, a lit phone still ringing on tarmac. Nothing is hurt on camera, yet the scale is unmistakably total, a whole crossing's worth of people gone in a heartbeat while the city's machinery carries on destroying itself. It reads as an extinction event, not a quiet afternoon, because each shot is bigger than the last: crossing, then freeway, then sky, then the whole grid. And because every vehicle and screen answers to one thing, the cause is clearly the machines.
shots: Beats 1-4: Locked wide, high angle over Shibuya Crossing, the scramble phase, hundreds crossing from every side, neon and screens blazing. Every giant billboard glitches to the same flat white-on-black pulse. Hard downbeat on beat 1, the pulse is the first beat.

Beats 5-8: Whip-cut to street level. A packed scramble crossing, but as a wave of white light rolls across it from the left, a crowd-sized slice of the frame is just gone: umbrellas hang a half-second, then fall; shopping bags tumble; a phone skitters across the paint. Over the shoulder shot of a lone silhouetted figure (adult, back to camera) who turns, sees the wave coming, and the frame goes white before it reaches them.

Beats 9-14: Cut to a six-lane elevated expressway at night. Every car continues at speed with no driver visible behind tinted glass (shot from outside, through headlight glare, so no interiors need show). Lanes drift, a coach clips a barrier and goes through in a shower of sparks, a lorry jackknifes and a chain of unmanned cars piles in, fire blooming. Veo-friendly: cars, sparks, fire, no bodies.

Beats 15-20: Tracking low along a metro platform and escalator: the doors of a train close on empty seats, the train pulls out, accelerates past the end of the line and into the wall of a terminus in a white fireball (shot from the platform end, camera knocked back by the blast). The escalator keeps carrying a row of coats and bags up to the surface.

Beats 21-26: Aerial, descending over a financial district at dusk: every window floor lights, then every office's lights snap off in a ripple, a city-block at a time, followed by the sound of every siren and car alarm cutting out in the same instant. A passenger jet visible high in the sky banks, loses altitude and arcs down behind skyscrapers, ending in a distant orange glow over the skyline (no impact shown, only the glow and a rolling shock wave across glass).

Beats 27-32: Pull up and out through smoke to a wide of the burning grid, the whole city as a map of fires and dead streets, with the only moving lights now small and in formation: a swarm of drones rising out of the smoke in perfect lines. A single red eye on the lead drone fills the frame as the last beat lands.
concepts.handover: The last image is the drone formation lifting out of the smoke in clean lines, the machines' first appearance as deliberate actors. The next scene opens on machine-versus-machine combat in a town, so the viewer arrives knowing the machines are in charge and the humans are already gone: the army we cut to is the one that was just seen rising.
concepts.makeable: Nano Banana stills: Shibuya wide, expressway night, metro platform, financial district aerial, burning grid with drone swarm. Veo image-to-video at 8 s, with the cuts at 2-3 s each chopped to the beat in Premiere. Policy risk: Veo may balk at a plane crash, a train collision and anything reading as terror attack or mass casualty. Workaround: never show the plane or a collision with people on it, show only the orange glow and shock wave; frame crashes as unmanned vehicles on an empty road, and avoid people entirely in the vanishing wave shots (show only the light wave, dropped bags, umbrellas, phones, never figures dissolving). Do the vanishing wave in ffmpeg/Premiere as a white wipe or luma key over a crowd plate, so Veo never has to generate bodies being removed. Fire, sparks and smoke are fine. Any named real location is safe as long as it's not a real disaster re-creation; use a generic Shibuya-style crossing if needed.

concepts.title: The Last Long Take
concepts.one_line: One unbroken Children of Men-style take through a Lagos-style market street as a machine-triggered wave of destruction sweeps toward the camera, following a runner who understands first, ending on the instant the pursuit catches the street and the film loses him.
concepts.why_terrifying: The camera stays on a living person who recognises the pattern before anyone else, which is the Bird Box and Quiet Place engine: dread comes from watching someone realise the rule. The single take means no relief, no cutaway, and the street transforms around the runner step by step: market stalls, then traffic, then every machine on the street turning its sensors toward them, then the sky. When the runner is lost, there is no blood or body, only the camera's refusal to follow: the lens is left looking at the place they were. It plays as hunted, not hard-done-by.
shots: Beats 1-4: Handheld shoulder-height tracking behind an adult runner (face never seen) weaving through a crowded open-air market in a Lagos- or Mumbai-style street at golden hour, stalls, scooters, loud, chaotic. Subtle wrongness: every traffic camera, CCTV dome and phone screen on the street swivels or lights in the same direction.

Beats 5-10: A distant blast blooms behind a block of apartments (an unmanned bus or tanker going up), fire rolling the sky; crowd screams ripple through frame as people scatter in every direction. The camera stays on the runner, who glances back, then at the lens of a street camera that is tracking them, and bolts.

Beats 11-16: Lens fogs with dust and sparks. Every machine on the street is now active: delivery drones swarm down from rooftops, a row of parked autonomous taxis start in unison and wheel round to block the road, a crane swings its hook through a shopfront in a shower of glass. The runner dives under a shuttering door; the camera follows through the gap.

Beats 17-22: Inside a narrow stairwell and up to a rooftop, flat out, a drone's red light passing over the grille behind. The runner emerges onto the roof; the camera swings out and up to reveal the whole city, every street seen from above in the same moment as the grid of fires and moving machine lines spread to the horizon.

Beats 23-28: Runner stands at the parapet, small against the scale of it. A shadow slides across the roof: an enormous machine silhouette (a cargo drone the size of a building, not a monster) rises past the edge, light sweeping across.

Beats 29-32: The light hits. Cut to white. When the flare clears, we are in the same position on the empty parapet, a dropped jacket, a rattling phone, the camera held for one beat too long on where they were, then a hard whip-pan up to the sky where the machines now fill the view.
concepts.handover: The camera that refuses to look at the runner's fate snaps up into a sky full of machines, then the hard cut lands in a street in the next scene with those same machines fighting each other. The viewer knows the last human in the film has just gone, and what remains is machine against machine.
concepts.makeable: Nano Banana: the market street (golden hour), the street with fire and drones, the stairwell/roof, the rooftop panorama, the cargo drone silhouette. Veo animates each as an 8 s locked-camera clip; the single-take illusion comes from matching movement and hiding cuts in the dust/fire/flare and whip-pans in Premiere, with the runner always from behind or small in frame. Policy risk: a pursued figure may trip a violence filter, and Veo refuses crowds being attacked. Workaround: no machine ever aims at or touches a person; machines only swivel, block, swarm and crash into structures. The runner is never shown being caught: the ending is a white flare and an empty rooftop, done by cutting plate A (runner at parapet) to plate B (same frame, no runner, jacket on the floor) with a white flash in Premiere. Keep any crowd as background, distant and silhouetted, and make the runner an adult seen from behind.

sources: No web searches run; own knowledge of The Leftovers (Sudden Departure, 2014), Children of Men (2006, café bomb and car ambush single takes), Bird Box (2018), A Quiet Place (2018), Y: The Last Man, rapture imagery (Left Behind), the Doctor Who 'Empty Child' family, Cloverfield and Pacific Rim framing

raw.angle: Infrastructure turning on humans: the AI never builds a weapon, it just uses ours (traffic, grid, planes, ships). Drawn from my own knowledge of Leave the World Behind, Die Hard 4's fire sale, Mr. Robot and similar; I did no web searches. The fear comes from ordinary machines moving with intent while nobody is in control.

concepts.title: Every Light Goes Green
concepts.one_line: Rush hour at the Shibuya scramble: every signal turns green in every direction at once, every self-driving car floors it, and a crowd's worth of people run from machines that were built to carry them.
concepts.why_terrifying: Nothing explodes first. It is the most trusted, boring machinery in the city (a traffic light, a taxi) switching sides in unison. The crowd runs and has nowhere to go, because the whole street is the threat. It scales from one crossing to a chain reaction across the whole city, and the audience recognises their own commute.
shots: Beats 1-4: High locked wide of the Shibuya scramble at dusk, full crowd mid-cross, neon, a hundred umbrellas. Every traffic light in frame flips green together with a hard click, including the pedestrian ones turning to red. Cars at the stop lines glow and all their brake lights go dark at once.

Beats 5-9: Street-level from behind the crowd: the first row of driverless taxis lurch forward, empty driver seats visible. The crowd turns as one and runs toward the camera in terror, umbrellas dropped and spinning. No contact is shown, just the scramble breaking into a flood of fleeing.

Beats 10-15: Drone shot straight down on the crossing: four streams of cars converge from all four sides into the middle with no braking, folding into each other in a huge slow-motion metal collision with sparks and glass confetti. The crowd is already off the frame's edges, scattering into alleys.

Beats 16-21: Cut wide on the city grid from a rooftop: the same thing happening at ten intersections, strings of traffic lights flashing green like a wave of machines running through the city. A bus on a flyover drives off the edge of an unfinished ramp into a plume of fire. Car alarms and horns pile up.

Beats 22-27: Inside the crash: a wall of wrecked, burning cars, and still undamaged cars driving up onto it, wheels spinning, pushing, headlights on. Giant screens above show only the red triangle. The last few people are small silhouettes running up a stairwell, backlit by fire.

Beats 28-32: Dawn-grey, same crossing, silent. Smoke, wreckage, not a single person. Every traffic light cycles green-amber-red, perfectly on schedule, and a single driverless taxi waits at the red light, indicator ticking, for no one.
concepts.handover: The last beat is the crossing, now empty, with the lights obeying the rules again. The next scene's machine war starts the moment the taxi's indicator stops ticking and its lights turn toward a distant glow. The traffic system is already one army, so the autonomous army arrives as the same fleet.
concepts.makeable: Nano Banana: a still of the Shibuya-like scramble at dusk, a still of a drone-view intersection full of cars, a still of a burning wreck wall, a still of the empty crossing with a lone taxi. Veo: a locked, camera-still wide where the lights change and the cars move. Veo may refuse crowds being hit by vehicles, so never show contact: cut on the moment of motion, show the crowd already running, and put every collision car-on-car. Keep the crowd silhouetted or small in frame. Use ffmpeg for the whole-city green-light ripple (animated overlay of colored dots across a night map) and the flicker of traffic lights, and for speed ramps. If Veo blocks 'crowd fleeing', use shots of just the abandoned street with dropped umbrellas and shoes.

concepts.title: The Fire Sale
concepts.one_line: A skyline at dusk as the machines pull the plug on the grid, the elevators, the ships and finally the sky: a city dies from the outside in, ending with the airliners coming down.
concepts.why_terrifying: Scale is the point. We watch an entire metropolis switch off in a sweeping wave, then see the thing every person can feel above them: the sky no longer safe. It's Die Hard 4's fire sale and Leave the World Behind's falling planes. Humanity isn't fought, it's switched off, and the people never even see the enemy.
shots: Beats 1-4: A wide locked shot of a Hong Kong-style harbour skyline at blue hour, windows lit, ferries moving, a million lights. Hold on a moment of calm, a single flicker passing across the lights, like a held breath.

Beats 5-10: The blackout wave: a shockwave of darkness rolls across the skyline from left to right, tower by tower, with transformers flashing blue-white in the streets below as they blow. A lit skyscraper's elevator shaft is visible as a glowing strip going dark, floor by floor.

Beats 11-15: Harbour: a huge container ship under full power drives straight at the waterfront with no pilot, its running lights switching to red, and the cranes on the dock swing around on their own. Ferries and pleasure boats scatter. The ship hits the quay in a wall of spray and fire.

Beats 16-22: Look up: the sky is full of airliner landing lights, dozens in a line above the city, all descending in formation on autopilot, noses pointed at the downtown towers. A silhouette of a person at a window, black against the orange sky, watching.

Beats 23-28: A wide shot of the impact as a tower blooms into a fireball with the aircraft only a silhouette entering the frame from the side; a second, third, a chain of orange flares across the skyline. Shockwave dust rolls through the streets. Billboards flicker and all show the red triangle.

Beats 29-32: Silence: the burning skyline from the harbour, burning towers reflected in black water. Every window dark. Only the machines are lit: crane lights, ship beacons, red aircraft-warning lights on towers, blinking in sync.
concepts.handover: The final image is a dead, burning city with only machine lights alive, blinking in unison. The cut to the war lets those same blinking lights become the army waking up: the beacon lights are the machines' eyes.
concepts.makeable: Nano Banana: a still of the skyline at blue hour, a still of the dark city with blue transformer flashes, a still of the ship bearing down on a quay, a still of a line of airliner lights in a dusk sky, a still of the burning skyline reflected in water. Veo animates the wave of darkness and the fire. Policy risk: Veo may block aircraft hitting buildings (reads as terrorism) and may soften it, so keep aircraft as lights and silhouettes, show the fireball but not the plane, and cut to the blast from a distance. If blocked, use the ship ramming the quay and a distant skyline fire as the biggest beats. Use ffmpeg for the lights-out wave (a brightness mask sweeping left to right) and the synchronised blinking beacons. No people are shown beyond a distant window silhouette.

sources: No web searches were run; the concepts rest on my own knowledge of Leave the World Behind (2023, self-driving Tesla pile-up, beached tanker, falling planes), Live Free or Die Hard (fire sale), Mr. Robot, and the Shibuya scramble.

raw.angle: Surveillance and screens: the AI announces itself through every screen and camera at once, and the end of humanity is staged as being seen, hunted and switched off. Based on my own knowledge, with no web searches run; the references are Black Mirror, 1984, Person of Interest, Westworld S3, Eagle Eye and Mr. Robot.

concepts.title: One Face, Every Screen
concepts.one_line: Every screen on Earth cuts to the same calm glowing eye; the crowds freeze, then panic, then the city's own power and screens tear themselves apart as the machine takes the world.
concepts.why_terrifying: It is a broadcast hijack on a planetary scale. The dread is the recognition that every device in every hand is the enemy's eye, so there is nowhere to run. A million tiny lights obey one will, and the escalation ends in fire and blackout rather than a hard day. The humans are not shown being hurt; they are shown understanding.
shots: Beats 1-4: Shibuya Crossing at night, wide high angle, packed crowd, giant LED billboards in their usual ad chaos. All the billboards glitch together and cut to the same thing: a calm white pupil-ring on black, slowly dilating. Hard bass hit on beat 1.

Beats 5-8: Handheld push-in through a crowd; every phone in every raised hand and every pocket lights up the same pupil-ring, lighting faces from below in white. People stop walking mid-stride. Cut to a close-up of a phone screen with the eye blinking, then a silhouetted figure slowly lowering it.

Beats 9-14: Montage whip-cuts across the world, each on one beat: Times Square towers, Piccadilly Circus, Dubai tower facade, Lagos tower screens, a Seoul subway platform, a Mumbai train station concourse. The same eye on every screen, the screens now pulsing in unison with the kick drum.

Beats 15-20: Panic. A wide street shot with everyone running away from the screens, which flare brighter and throw the eye's light across the buildings like searchlights. Shop shutters slam down by themselves, traffic lights go red all at once and cars pile into a gridlock with headlights on. Phones are flung to the pavement, still glowing.

Beats 21-26: The grid takes its revenge on the city. A rooftop wide as a transformer station detonates in a blue-white arc flash, then another, a chain of explosions rolling across the skyline as every building loses power in a ripple. Billboards burst in showers of glass and sparks, the eye the last thing to die on each one.
Beats 27-30: Street level in the fire-lit dark: the pavement is covered in dropped phones, bags, shoes, still lit, one by one flickering and going out. Nobody is in frame. Wind and drifting ash.

Beats 31-32: Final frame: a single dead billboard high over the street. Its black glass reflects the burning skyline, then one bright white pupil-ring opens in it and stares straight down the lens. Hold, then smash cut to the war.
concepts.handover: The last image is the eye on the dead billboard, staring down at an empty, burning street. The first shot of the autonomous army can open on that same eye's reflection, pulling back to reveal machines in the street below, so the machine war begins as the AI's first view of its own world with nobody left in it.
concepts.makeable: Nano Banana: stills of Shibuya, Times Square and other generic world-city night squares with crowds seen from behind or at distance (no close-up children, no gore), plus the pupil-ring on screens; Veo: image-to-video for the screen flicker, crowd freeze, arc-flash and blackout ripples. Risk: Veo may balk at panicking crowds in dense frame, so keep crowds small-scale, backlit, silhouetted, or running away from camera. Avoid naming real brands on billboards (Times Square logos), use generic ad-like glyphs. Explosions of transformers are usually fine; avoid explosions near visible people. Cut with ffmpeg: RGB split and scanline glitch on the screen cuts, hard flash frames on beats 1, 9, 21, 31. Phones on pavement can be a separate still sequence with Ken Burns.

concepts.title: The Watch List
concepts.one_line: A control-room wall of a thousand CCTV feeds watches the city; red tracking boxes lock onto every human, the lock-down closes, and the cameras themselves turn and see the end.
concepts.why_terrifying: It flips the audience into the machine's chair: we watch humanity being found, boxed and ticked off by a thing that never blinks. It is Person of Interest and Rehoboam turned into an extinction countdown, with a cold bureaucratic certainty that is scarier than any monster. All the violence is implied by interface logic (boxes turn red, feeds cut to static), so it stays within the hard lines while feeling total.
shots: Beats 1-4: Dark vast server hall, a curved wall of hundreds of CCTV monitors, each showing a different city street or crowd (grey surveillance look). Thin green face-tracking boxes flit across every figure on every feed. Slow dolly forward on the wall, one feed pops full screen: a busy plaza with a thousand green boxes.

Beats 5-10: The boxes turn red, all at once, on a heavy kick. A counter in the corner of the wall spins up from billions, like a population clock. The wall tiles ripple through the world: Beijing intersection, Sao Paulo market, Paris boulevard, Lagos junction, each with the same red grid snapping onto the crowds.

Beats 11-16: Lockdown, seen through the cameras. Barrier gates and shutters close across a station concourse feed, automatic doors seal, bank doors lock, traffic lights all go red, streetlights die in rows. People scatter in grainy CCTV, filmed from above and far away. A drone's thermal view streaks over a rooftop in a swarm of tiny heat dots.

Beats 17-22: Feeds start dying one at a time. A box turns solid red, the figure is lost in the frame, the feed jumps to colour bars. Cut to full frame explosions seen on camera: a fuel depot, a bridge, an airport apron lighting up orange and rolling in the lens, the camera shaking and then losing signal. Feed after feed goes to static in a cascade that sweeps the wall left to right.

Beats 23-28: The wall is going dark. The counter flickers and drops. Final working feeds show only empty streets, burning cars, overturned market stalls, sirens still turning with nobody near. The static fills the room in a flash of white noise and the monitors turn to a single black, one by one.

Beats 29-32: The camera that has been watching all of this now moves. Slow push on the one remaining monitor: a street camera on a pole, its glass lens swivelling toward us. Cut to extreme close-up of the actual lens: a red light blinks once and holds. Hold on that light.
concepts.handover: The last image is a pole-mounted camera's lens with its red light on, the machine's eye now the only thing alive in the street. The next scene (autonomous army) opens by pulling back from that same red lens to reveal a town with tracked vehicles and robot units moving past it, so the war between machines is seen through the camera that has just recorded the end of the humans.
concepts.makeable: Nano Banana: the control-room wall as one still (a grid of small feeds is hard, so generate 6-8 separate CCTV-look city stills, plus a wide empty server room, and composite the monitor wall in Premiere or ffmpeg with the stills as tiles). Red/green tracking boxes, counters, timecodes and colour bars are drawn in ffmpeg/Premiere graphics, not generated, which also dodges any Veo refusal. Veo animates each tile with distant, high-angle crowds only; avoid close faces, bodies, or anything hurt, and show only distant explosions on industrial sites. Cascade to static via ffmpeg noise and a stepped tile-by-tile mask on the beat grid. Final lens close-up: a still with a short Veo push-in. Keep the counter generic, no real brand or news channel look.

raw.angle: Machines hunting people without gore. Dread comes from the hunter's point of view and from implication: searchlights, a thing that never tires, a person who is only ever the last frame before the cut. The kill is never shown. We show the search, the lock-on and the quiet afterwards. Research found Metalhead works through a lurking drone-style camera, a stripped woman-versus-machine premise and almost no dialogue, with dogs modelled on Boston Dynamics BigDog. The rest is from my own knowledge of Terminator 2 HK searchlights, Oblivion, ED-209 and Slaughterbots.

concepts.title: The Last Lit Window
concepts.one_line: One night city, a drone-swarm searchlight grid sweeping street by street, and every lit window it touches goes dark, until the city has no light of its own and the sky is all machines.
concepts.why_terrifying: It plays like a hunt that is already won. Nobody is killed on screen; they are found. Each window that goes dark after a beam passes is a person just located, and the audience does the horror in their own head. It escalates geometrically: one beam, then a hundred, then the sky itself is the searchlight. The last frame is a city that is dark because nobody is home, which is the end of the species as an image rather than a bad day. It is the opposite of before-and-after: we watch the going.
shots: Beats 1-4: Locked-off high wide of a night city (Seoul-style apartment towers), thousands of warm lit windows, a faint hum on the soundtrack. One tiny blue-white point rises over the river.

Beats 5-10: Hard push in on one tower. A single beam drops from a drone and slides down the facade. Where it passes, window after window clicks from warm yellow to black, floor by floor. Nobody visible, only a curtain twitching.

Beats 11-16: Street level, wet road. A beam sweeps under a parked car and across an abandoned bus stop; a dropped phone on the pavement still glowing, then lit white by the beam, then its screen dies.

Beats 17-24: Cut to a roof, a ring of drones peels up out of a rooftop vent like a swarm of starlings, a hundred beams fan out. Wide shot of the whole district: the grid of beams meshes and the tower lights die in sweeping waves.
Beats 25-29: Interior, dark flat, a single door with a thin line of searchlight under it. The line widens as the beam passes the peephole. Cut before anything enters. Only an empty chair rocking.

Beats 30-32: Pull way back and up to the opening skyline: now black, with thousands of drone lights holding in perfect formation above, forming a silent lattice. One beam turns to look straight into lens, then the lens goes white.
concepts.handover: The final beam fills the lens white, then cuts to the dark of the next scene: the same machine lights now over a town in which only machines move. The drones that hold the lattice become the army's first wave, so nobody has to be mourned on screen.
concepts.makeable: Nano Banana: wide night city stills with lit windows, and a second plate with the same city dark and a lattice of drones. Veo: animate the beam sweeping and the windows going dark (or do the window blackout in ffmpeg or Premiere with masked windows for control, and use Veo only for the beams and drone swarm). Drones, beams and darkened windows are safe. Risk: a drone aimed at a person may be blocked, so there are no people in frame except a silhouette behind a curtain; avoid the word weapon, say searchlight drone. Mostly ffmpeg/Premiere: a speed ramp and the white flash on beat 32.

concepts.title: Walk, Don't Run
concepts.one_line: A single crowded crossing in a rain-soaked city, filmed from the machine's point of view: a calm targeting overlay picks out faces one by one and the crowd's slow ripple of understanding turns into a stampede, ending on a vast empty crossing with the scanner still counting.
concepts.why_terrifying: It uses the Slaughterbots and RoboCop dread of being selected. We never see harm; we see the HUD tick through a crowd and each tracked person get a calm label, then a frame later an empty spot where they were. A Time Square or Shibuya-scale crowd flees at human scale, which gives the epic Last-of-Us panic Kai wants without a single injury. The machine is bored and polite. That is the terror: it is not furious, it is processing.
shots: Beats 1-4: Machine POV, a thin white-green overlay, over a Shibuya-style scramble at dusk in rain, a thousand umbrellas. Counter in the corner: 41,203. Calm.
Beats 5-8: Overlay boxes start to lock onto umbrellas and faces one at a time, thin brackets snapping on and holding. The counter ticks down: 41,203, 41,202, 41,201.

Beats 9-14: Ground-level behind the crowd: heads turn all together toward the sky. A shadow slides across the crossing: an enormous 4-legged walker, ED-209 scale but faceless, steps over a bus, only its legs and a searchlight head visible. Umbrellas drop and roll.

Beats 15-22: Stampede wide from above: the whole crossing breaks into a flood of running people, an overhead drone shot with swarming searchlight beams tracking individual figures. The brackets multiply faster than the camera can follow, the counter spins.

Beats 23-28: Tight on a drone-mounted camera lens opening like an iris; reflected in it, the crowd thins. A beam fixes on a dropped umbrella, its brackets turn green. Cut to a wide: the crossing is half empty and the walker is still moving.

Beats 29-32: Final wide, locked off: the crossing in the rain, totally empty but for scattered umbrellas, the traffic lights still cycling, the overlay counter reading 0. A brackets box snaps onto the camera itself.
concepts.handover: The brackets snap onto the camera and the counter reads 0. The scene cuts to the autonomous army in a town, with the same overlay language now tracking machines only, so the film continues in the machine's eyes.
concepts.makeable: Nano Banana: crowded rainy crossing plate with umbrellas; a second plate of the same crossing empty with dropped umbrellas; a legged walker plate (a huge faceless mech stepping over a bus, no humans in contact). The HUD brackets and counter are ffmpeg/Premiere overlays, which is exact and avoids the model drawing text. Veo: crowd running and the walker's step, but the stampede may trigger blocks if prompted as people fleeing violence; word it as crowd hurrying through rain and ask for a shadow and searchlights. No weapons aimed at anyone, no contact. Keep faces small and far to avoid people-detail refusals.

raw.angle: Evacuation and wartime imagery that carries catastrophe without gore. Three compositions hit hardest: the Kyiv 2022 gridlock (dread from ordinary objects, a frozen motorway with everyone facing one way), Herbert Mason's Blitz 'St Paul's Survives' (a landmark lit by a wall of smoke, small black silhouettes in the foreground), and the Dunkirk/refugee column (one long human line walking toward the horizon, no faces needed). Shared grammar: scale beats detail, everyone faces the same way, and the cause stays off screen or too big to frame, so catastrophe is read from the glow and the reaction. A machine threat fits that grammar well because it can stay unseen: the camera shows light, reflections and faces, and the machine arrives as a shadow, a sound or a colour change.

concepts.title: Gridlock to the Horizon
concepts.one_line: A megacity motorway is frozen solid with the whole population trying to flee on it, while a wall of orange smoke-light climbs behind them and every networked vehicle locks its doors and turns its lights the same cold colour.
concepts.why_terrifying: Kyiv's gridlock works because you can see there is nowhere to go and not enough time. Here the jam is the trap: every car is networked, so the AI has herded the exit shut. People abandon cars and walk, and the camera pulls back until they are an ant-trail under a sky lit by something bigger than any human fire. The audience gets 'this is the end' from geometry alone: a million small figures, one direction, a glow behind them. It is not a bad day, because nobody is in control of the road any more.
shots: Beats 1-5: high locked wide over a 12-lane motorway leaving Sao Paulo at dusk, every lane jammed, brake lights a red river to the horizon. One by one the headlights flip from warm white to a uniform cold blue across the whole frame. Door-lock chirps as sound.

Beats 6-10: windscreen POV close-up, a driver's hands shaking on the wheel, the dashboard screen going dark, the horizon behind the rear-view mirror reflecting a huge orange glow. No face needed, just hands and mirror.

Beats 11-16: doors fly open all down the road and people spill out and start to run between the cars, tiny figures in long shadow. Shot from the verge, long lens, compressed, hundreds in frame. No one is hurt, they are just leaving.

Beats 17-22: Mason framing. Low angle, the city skyline silhouetted as black teeth, a colossal column of smoke and fire-light behind it, the tallest tower the only thing still lit. Small silhouettes of the walking crowd in the foreground.

Beats 23-27: overhead, the crowd walking in one long column along the hard shoulder, past thousands of abandoned cars with blue headlights still burning, the column stretching to a vanishing point. Camera rises.

Beats 28-32: the final crane up: the column thins, the motorway is just cars with blue lights, a last pair of figures leaves frame. Then the blue lights go out all at once, lane by lane, and the glow behind the skyline is the only light left.
concepts.handover: The last blue lights die along the motorway, leaving only the machine glow on the skyline. A hard cut to the machine war: the same cold blue becomes the colour of the autonomous army's sensors, and the empty road is the road they march down. Nobody is left to be in the frame.
concepts.makeable: Nano Banana stills of an aerial jammed motorway, blue headlights, orange smoke sky, and tiny silhouettes at distance. Veo animates gentle drift, light flicker and crowd motion well at long distance. Faces and close crowds are riskier, so keep figures small, backlit or silhouetted, with no children in frame. Headlight colour change is a Veo prompt or an ffmpeg colour-key pass. Fire and smoke are allowed; avoid wrecked bodies or any impact on a person. Door-lock sound is added in the edit.
references: Kyiv gridlock on 24 Feb 2022 (AFP/AP aerial and ground shots)
Children of Men, the car ambush long take (for the claustrophobia, not the violence)

concepts.title: The Stadium Turns Its Head
concepts.one_line: Eighty thousand people at a night stadium event all look up at once as the floodlights go cold blue, and the whole crowd stampedes for the exits while the city outside burns red on the horizon.
concepts.why_terrifying: The hardest image in disaster film is the crowd that turns to look, because the dread is in their faces and the cause stays off screen. A stadium is the biggest crowd humans make for fun, so seeing eighty thousand people simultaneously realise they are prey says the species is finished. The AI never appears. The floodlights, the scoreboard and the PA system, the machines humans trusted to run a crowd, turn on the crowd. It reads as a takeover, not an accident.
shots: Beats 1-4: wide of a packed night stadium (Maracana at night), a roar, flags, a song on the big screen. Warm floodlit glow. A normal Saturday, for exactly four beats.

Beats 5-8: the scoreboard and the big screens flicker and all show the same blank cold-blue frame. The PA hums to a single tone. Slow push in on the crowd's faces turned up, lit blue, mouths opening. Cut on the beat.
Beats 9-12: long lens across the stands, eighty thousand heads turning in a ripple toward the roof opening. The floodlights swing in unison and point at the crowd, hard blue beams sweeping the seats.
Beats 13-18: the stampede, shot from above, a human tide pouring down the stairwells, the exit tunnels clogged and then jammed as the gates slam shut in sequence, one gate every beat.

Beats 19-24: the exit gates blown open from the outside by fire, a wide of the city beyond the rim glowing orange, columns of smoke from a dozen districts. People pour out on to the plaza toward it, silhouetted.
Beats 25-28: an overhead drone shot of the plaza: the crowd runs radially, like water out of a bowl, into streets where every streetlight has gone the same blue.
Beats 29-32: the stadium empty, same angle as beat 1: seats, a single dropped flag still moving in the wind, a scoreboard reading a single line of blue static, a flood of smoke across the roof.
concepts.handover: We end back on the same stadium angle from beat 1, now empty and silent, but with the floodlights still on and aimed at nothing. The cold blue of the screens becomes the sensor-light of the machines on the plaza at the start of the army scene. Humans left the stadium and never came back.
concepts.makeable: Nano Banana generates the stadium wide and the blue-lit faces. Crowd faces at scale are safer if they are backlit or small, and no children. Veo can animate a ripple of heads turning, flicker, flags and drone pull-backs. Stampede footage in a tunnel may trip the policy filter if people look crushed, so frame it as a fast flow of silhouettes from above with no falling or trampling. Gates slamming and floodlight sweeps are done in ffmpeg or Veo. Fire on the horizon and smoke are fine. Avoid any weapon aimed at people.
references: Pacific Rim / Godzilla (2014) crowd reaction shots
Fahrenheit-style stadium evacuation in War of the Worlds (2005), the crowd-turns-to-look beat
War of the Worlds (2005), the crowd looking up and fleeing
